Before we proceed with these estimates, may I ask when we may expect to receive the fourth volume of the Auditor General's Report which is supposed to contain the detailed expenditure of the Department of Militia?

I cannot answer with respect to the Auditor General's Report, but a memorandum on the organization of the whole department, which was spoken of the other day, when the Militia expenditures were referred to, is in the bands of the printer and I understand will be available at the end of this week or the beginning of next.

The Auditor General's Report, containing the details of the Militia expenditure for last year, is what we are asking for. It contains the only data we have upon which to base our criticisms of the estimates for the present year.
Does the hon. gentleman say that the fourth volume of the Auditor General's Report has not yet been brought dowm?
It has not been laid on the Table and has not been distributed.
In that case it may not be available for some time.

The report of the Militia Council has been brought down, .and also the memorandum to which I referred. The latter does not contain any data as regards expenditure, but deals more with the organization of the whole department.
Will the minister give us some explanation of the reduction of $30,000 as compared with the estimates of last year? How is the item made up?

As my hon. friend is aware, having been in the Militia, the militia Units in Canada have had very little assistance since the war started. In 1914 and 1915 the Active Militia units were the basis and foundation for the whole Canadian Expeditionary Force, and last year they were pretty well knocked to pieces all over the country. After pro-, viding for organization, allowance for pay, instruction, care of arms, and so forth, it is estimated that we can do with $30,000 less this year than last year.

Where are these arms stored?
Major-General MEWBURN:	They are
kept in the armouries of the corps. A very large number of |he Militia units have kept their organizations together, and last year and the year before they were parading and drilling, particularly the city corps, at least once a week and keeping up to their old peace establishment. These units are mainly composed of men who are medically unfit, and they carry on their summer training. This is not so much the case with the rural corps, because they have not been in camp.

Is it the minister's intention to see to it that all militia officers now employed in the active militia are given the opportunity to serve overseas if they wish to?
Major-General MEWBURN:	They not
only have been given the opportunity; they have been urged. In fact, I think the Militia officers who have held commissions since 1914 will probably be a little more than requested tto join the ranks in the Canadian Expeditionary Force. Since the Military Service Act came into operation, nc commissions have been given in the active militia, none at all. That clause in the proposed amendment embraces those who did not get to the actual theatre of war, and militia officers within the ages called. In fact, I am glad to say that a very large number of these officers- have joined the ranks.

Did I understand the minister to say that a large number of officers in the training corps are still employed training men who are medically unfit to go overseas?
Major-General MEWBURN: No; I said that in several of the city corps throughout Canada the corps have given far more than their establishment to the overseas service. Then, in these regiments, there are still a considerable number of men who were medically unfit or over or under age who still retained their identity with the active militia. These units in many cases have filled up their ranks with other men. For instance, members of Canadian and Rotary clubs joined these militia units at the time of the home guard movement, and have carried on their training without any pay, and have done a certain amount of musketry training on Saturday afternoons in the summer. In this way, many units have ' kept their organization together, and they were very largely the organizations which helped so well with voluntary recruiting.

A large number of these
militia units could be very easily abolished, and the expense of their training saved. We have in Quebec a composite battalion composed, I understand, of the old 8th and 9th Battalions. I suppose there are some ten or fifteen officers and three or four hundred men. If the men are fit, why not send them overseas? If they are unfit, why keep them in uniform?
Major-General MEWBURN: For the information of the hon. member, so far as the unit he speaks of is concerned, any men in it who are medically fit will go overseas. Those who are not medically fit in all these units-there are some in Quebec and in other districts, some of which are known as . Special Service Companies-we are organizing now what is known as a Garrison Regiment, -which will absorb any of these men who are not required for overseas service. [DOT] I hope that the unit referred to by my hon. friend will disappear off the horizon altogether.

I did not refer to the Quebec unit only. I understand there are a large number of militia units.
Major-General A1EWBURN:	They have
been very materially cut down. There has-been one on the Welland canal, and one at the Soo.

And one at Lachine canal.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I do not
know. There is one at Sault Ste. Marie, and there is a corps on the internment operations at Kapuskasing and at other points. And there were some that we have relieved and done away with in British Columbia. There is still a corps at Esquimalt and one at Halifax, but these have been practically reduced to nothing.

Is the expense incurred by their maintenance under this heading?
Major-General MEWBURN:	No, it is
not.
Cadet services-For pay of instructors, expenses of teadhers qualifying- at (Military Solioois and contingent expenses-$75,000.

Will the minister explain
what that item is for and what is going to be done with this money during the present year?
Major-General MEWBURN:	The object
of this vote is to maintain the different cadet units and encourage the cadet services throughout the country. It includes pay and allowances and transportation of organizers and inspectors amounting to

$27,000. The instruction allowances total $47,000; physical training course for school teachers, $600; and 'oonjtingent expenses $400. The expenditure for the year 1917-18 was estimated at $90,000, and this year a saving of $15,000 will probably be effected by a reduction of the instruction allowances It seems in the interest of the country that these cadet corps, which are a very goodi organization all over Canada, should not be allowed to go to pieces.

How many are in the cadet corps in Montreal?
Major-General iMEWBURN: I would not like to give the actual numbers; I think there are about 150 or 160 corps throughout Canada. Xn some plades they are stronger than in others. They are really run in connection with schools and colleges.

The organization- known as the Boy 'Scouts does not come under this vote?
Major-General iMEWBURN: No.

Is there any money paid
by the department to the Boy Scouts?
Major-General IMEWBURN: No, there is not. A good many of the Boy Scouts are members of the cadets.

Are these cadet corps
furnished with rifles and other necessary equipment?
Major-General MEWBURN:	A number
of the Ross cadet rifles are furnished to some of them. Of course, these rifles had to- be taken away from the cadet corps to be used for training purposes, but I am glad to say they have been handled back to the cadet corps. They are in charge of the different -schools.

What was done with the Ross rifles taken from the rifle associations? Are they available now? If so, the rifle association of the town of Renfrew would -like to receive their rifles back. There is -a c-or-ps there of 100 members, and they have done good .service. I would like to know if these rifles will be returned to the association.
Major-General -MEWBURN: I would not guarantee that they will. The rifles which had -been loaned to these associations had to be withdrawn, and it may be possible -to give some of these associations the loan of some rifles- this summer.
[Major-General Mewburn.]

The members of the association have been disappointed because the rifles were taken away from them.
Major-General MEWBURN:	The rifles
-were required and- the Ross cadet rifles also had to he withdrawn from the cadets for training purposes, and there are other reasons which I do- n-o-t think I wrould be at -liberty to give, tout I would -be glad to explain them -to my hon. friend.

I am greatly interested
in this question, because I was captain of the association at Renfrew for -many years. Many members of our association enlisted and have done good service at the front. Are these rifles to- be made available again, [DOT]so that the organization may resume its work?
The minister could obtain a large number of rifles from the Montreal Home Guard Association, an institutiop which was stifled in its birth. My rifle is available if my hon. friend wants it.

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: The rifle that the home guard were using is not at all suited for active service.
Is it not useful for target practice?

speakerposition: Minister of Marine and Fisheries; Minister of the Naval Service
speechtext: It is not very good.
It is called the Savage rifle-the name is rather significant. While the Ross rifle Mark I/II was not so efficient for actual service at the front, it was very useful for target practice.

Who is inspector of cadets for the district of Quebec?
Major-General MEWBURN: Major Pa-quet.

What is Major Paquet's military record? Has he been overseas?
Major-General MEWBURN: I understand that he was declared medically unfit.

Was he not in command of an overseas battalion a few years ago?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I am informed that he was in command of an overseas unit at one time, but that he did not proceed overseas because of his being medically unfit.

Did his battalion proceed overseas?
Major-General MEWBURN: In drafts, I am informed.

If he is physically unfit, how can he hold this position?

Major-General MEWBURN: He is only a cadet instructor, drawing no pay or emolument.

Is any school or college throughout the Dominion that makes application entitled to allowance in respect of cadet corps?
Major-General MEWBURN: Any school that has a cadet corps officially organized and authorized can get the allowance.

Who authorizes the organization of the cadet corps?
Major-General MEWBURN: It is recommended in the usual way to the Minister of Militia and Council and approved here.

By the Minister of Militia or the department?
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes.

I have seen the boys training at Mount Allison University in my own town, and I have wondered whether they were receiving assistance from the Militia Department. What is the extent of the allowance?
Major-General MEWBURN: One dollar per cadet, and fifty cents each for those in excess of fifty in each corps.

That applies to any cadet corps properly organized, which makes application in the usual way to the Militia Department?	*
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes.

Who is inspector of cadets for the Alontreal district?
Major-General AIEWBURN: Aly deputy -informs me that there is none at present.

Is it the intention of the department to have one?
Alajor-General AIEWBURN: I understand that one of the staff officers of Alilitary District No. 4 is temporarily carrying on.

Is there an inspector of cadets in New Brunswick?
Alajor-General MEWBURN: I think there are eleven inspectors altogether, one in each military district. New Brunswick now constitutes Military District No. 7; it formerly formed part of Alilitary District No. 6-New Brunswick, Nova Scotia, and Prince Edward Island.

Is there any truth in the report that some of the cadet corps have been deprived of their rifles?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Alark III
cadets rifles were called in all over for use
in training in the C.E.F. We have taken [DOT]steps to have these all replaced. The cadet corps only were not deprived of rifles; the rifles were withdrawn from all militia units throughout Canada for the same purpose.
Militia and Defence-departmental library,

Are the honorary colonels admitted to the library?
Major-General MEWBURN: The library may be open to all respectable citizens of Canada, but I am not aware that any honorary colonels have ever taken- advantage of the opportunity of studying military law.

The minister's answer
prompts another suggestion. Since we are in the midst of a multiplication of departments and boards, would it not be well for the minister to appoint a board to make -what shall I call it?
Some hon. AIEMBERS: A cleaning up.
Major-General MEWBURN:	Grading.

No, I would not grade
them; I would clean up a few hundred of [DOT]them. This board might inquire whether [DOT]these honorary colonels are going to continue to parade round the country without rendering any military service.
The reason I say this is that I do not think it is fair to those men who are real, genuine colonels, who devote themselves to the defence of this country and who work for the country, who have other men, who are only honorary colonels, graded with them. I do not mean to say that the honorary colonels are not honest citizens; I do not mean to say they do not deserve the rank they have been given, but I do not like to see a man who hasi never opened a law book in hie life proclaimed Doctor of Laws by a university. It is not fair to those who have studied law, and1 I am sure the minister, who has been before the courts, hammering away at law practically all his life, will agree with me. The same thing ought to be true with regard to the genuine colonel and the " Turkish rug " or " parlour carpet " colonel. It would be a good move to appoint a board of examiners and have a clean-up of these honorary colonels.
Militia and Defence-engineer servioes and works, $430,000.
Major-General MEWBURN:	There has
been a reduction of $135,500.

Will this include any
work that might be done to the walls of the city of Quebec?

Major-General MEWBURN:	Yes. The
item covers ordinary repairs and works; Halifax defences, Quebec defences, Esquimau defences and so on. The upkeep of the Quebec defences is estimated to cost $26,000.

How is the work done?
iMajor-General MEWBURN:	By day
labour.

Was any money spent
at St. John?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I do not
think so.

Why is it that those repairs on the Quebec defences amounting last year to $50,000 were carried out by day labour instead of tenders being called for?
Major-General MEWBURN: As ,we have our own engineer services in charge of the work, probably that is the cheapest way in which, so far as the Government is concerned, it can be done. It is probably cheaper than having a regular contract.

Is it not the general policy of the Government that, for any work amounting to over $5,000, tenders must be called for and contracts let? Is there not an Order in Council to that effect?
Major-General MEWBURN: I do not think this $26,000 is for one particular piece of work. It is for all the work on the permanent defences.

I understand that every year ' a certain amount, exceeding $10,000, is spent for repairs on the walls. Why was that work not given by tender and contract? Is the minister not of the opinion that it would save the Government a great deal of trouble and the public
10 p.m. a great deal of expense if the policy was adopted of letting all that repair work by tender and contract instead of having it done by day labour?
Major-General MEWIBURN: In some instances, owing to military exigencies, it is necessary to have work done in a hurry, and it might be quicker to have it done by day labour, and I am informed that in ordinary repairs more economy is shown by having the work done through the engineer services. I quite agree with' my hon. friend that in the ordinary course work ought to be done by tender and contract.

I am not aware of what goes on in 'other cities, but during an election campaign, for instance, on the. day imme-

diately preceding an election, I have seen an army of labourers working on repairs to the walls of the city of Quebec, and the very day after fee election the repairs were stopped. If the minister looks into the matter, he will find out from the accounts of his department that my statement is correct.
Major-General MEWBURN: I shall be very glad to look into the matter, but probably some of the work belongs to another department. Is my hon. friend referring to general work?

I am referring to the work done on the fortifications of Quebec.
Major-General MEWBURN: I thought my hon. friend was referring to general work.

No. I could make the same remark as regards the Marine and Fisheries Department or the Public Works Department, hut I am now referring to the fortifications of Quebec. I do not object to the labouring classes of any city in Canada getting work during an election or at any other time, but it would be good policy to see that such work is not used as a political bribe.
I am. rather surprised that this work should be done in Quebec during the election. I thought work of this kind was done only in doubtful constituencies.

I see in the details of this item that ordinary repairs and works will amount this year to $269,000, as against $345,500 last year. Will the minister give us some explanation as to this item?
Major-General MEWBURN: These estimates are for ordinary repairs and works in Military District No. 1, $10,000; Military District No. 2, that is Toronto, $23,000; Military District No. 3, $12,000; Military District No. 4, $20,000; Military District No. 5, $40,000; Military District No. 6, $10,000; Military District No. 7, $5,000; Military District No. 10, $14,000; Military District No. 11, $6,000; Military District No. 12, $4,000, and Military District No. 13, $5,000. Those are the estimated requirements of the various districts. The amount has been cut down to what is estimated as the lowest possible minimum.

I wanted to get ffom the
minister the details of the items that come under that title.
Major-General MEWTBURN:	I have just
given them...

(Mr. VIEN: The hon. minister has given the expenditure in each district.
Major-General MEWBTJRN:	No, the estimated expenditure that would 'be required.

I would like to know what
is meant by " ordinary repairs and works " What work, and what repairs?
Major-General MEWBTJRN:	I am more
familiar with military district No. 2, and I may say that we have repairs to ar-moAies, Stanley (barracks, and such as that. There are many armouries where local repairs are performed by engineers. Some of the main repairs, for instance putting on a new roof or anything like that, would be chargeable to Public Works, but the 'engineer service has the care of all the armouries throughout the various districts, and the expenditures has been much heavier particularly while the war is on. This year they can be reduced considerably. One or two armouries have been fitted up with bunks, and so on, which has been done by the engineer service.

Would that include roads?
For instance the road from Quebec to Val-cartier camp?
Major-General MEWBTJRN:	No. When
we speak of roads, the only road I know of, off hand, is the road at the barracks at Kingston. I think there was work done around there.

I think the same remarks
I made a minute ago, as to the defences, apply to those repairs and works. Will the minister be prepared to say that no repairs or works involving an expenditure of more than $5,000 has*been done by day work, and that such works have been carried on by tender, and contract?
Major-General MEWBTJRN:	My experience in the districts is that any expenditure over $5,000 has always been awarded by contract, we have always had three independent valuations.

Will the whole item of
$269,000 be expended?
Major-General MEWBTJRN: I would not say it would all be expended. Where we have the engineers in the camps and sapper labour, a good deal- of the work can be done much more expeditiously by them.

The small works could be more expeditiously or properly carried out by day labour, but when it comes to any amount over $5,000, I think the House
would like to have assurance from the minister that no expenditure will be authorized before tenders are called for.
Major-General MEWBTJRN: I can assure the hon. member, so far as my knowledge goes, that I think-I will not say positively, because I am not speaking with perfect certainty for the past-that in all cases of $5,000 or over contracts have been let. Where a contract has not been advertised, there have been at least three independent valuations, which have been submitted to headquarters, before being accepted, and the job has been done by day work as a rule. But while the war is on there have been many matters of an urgent nature which come under the engineer service. I know of many urgent cases, such as the fitting up of military hospitals. Take the case of the Exhibition Camp in Toronto; the work has been done by the engineers and sapper labour, and we simply bought the material. If we had let the work by contract, it would have cost more money, and would not have been done as rapidly.

I suppose the repairs to public works at the Engineers' Camp at Levis come under that item?
Major-General MEWBTJRN: I think so.

Could the hon. minister tell me how much was expended last year on that camp?
Major-General MEWBTJRN: I have not that information before me.

I will cite that case to my hon. friend. Almost every year several thousand dollars are spent at the Engineers Camp at Levis. I do not complain of that, but I complain of the fact that it is always done by day work.
Major-General MEWBTJRN: The hon. gentleman thinks it had better be done by contract?

Surely, and I think that is the policy to be adopted for every expenditure coming under the control of the department. We are at war, and are spending tremendous amounts of money lavishly for all sorts of things. I know for a fact that in various instances money has been badly spent, and works have been constructed that had to be torn down. I am quite sure that if a proper supervision of the expenditure had taken place hundreds of thousands of dollars could have been saved, and I think the Empire would be just as safe, and Canada would be better off. I submit to my hon. friend that in

future this policy should be carried out. Can the hon. gentleman tell me whether any of these expenses, amounting last year to over ?345,000, covers any expenditure concerning the Eoss rifle in Quebec?
Major-General MEWBURN: Not at all.

Or repairs to or changes in the building?
Major-General MEWBURN: No.

I understand some expenditure was made in connection with the Ross rifle. Can the hon. gentleman tell me under what vote it comes, and if it is shown in the estimates.
Major-General MEWBURN: I know of nothing in the estimates except that we have an inspection 'branch in the building, the expense of which is charged to the appropriation, but nothing in these estimates.

I know the Ross rifle in Quebec has been discarded to a certain extent, and they 'are now used at the barracks by the men. UndeT what head in the estimates come the expenditure incurred in connection therewith?
Major-General MEWBURN: That is a war appropriation estimate-nothing to do with this.
(Mr. POWER: I understand that in connection with these engineering works the department is obliged at times to make certain purchases. I presume that they would have to purchase pickaxes, shovels, paint brushes and that kind of thing. Will the hon. minister express the laudable intention of some the other ministers, notably the Minister of Marine .and Fisheries (Mr. Bal-lantyne), 'and tell us whether ox not in his department he intends to abolish the patronage list? I know that for many years in Quebec they had patronage lists, and when any purchases were to be made by the Militia Department certain men were asked for tenders. On looking over the Auditor General's Report this year, I am sorry to find the same principle seems to obtain. For instance, all the plumbing was done by one man, and almost all the painting toy another mian, and so on. I would like to suggest to the minister that he give a similar statement to that made by the Minister of Marine and Fisheries, that in future all patronage whatsoever will be abolished.
Major-General MEWBURN: I will go a little further and say that when I took

office 'as Minister of Militia on 12th October last, I did abolish all patronage, and I intend to 'follow out that poilicy as long as I have the honour to be in office. As far as I am aware those purchases were made through the War Purchasing Coimmiseion. And I may say, not only with regard to the purchases, but with regard to any other matter in connection with the Department of Militia and Defence, I certainly will hold up both hands for the abolition of patronage, and I intend to always carry out that policy.

I was referring to the small purchases made in the various districts. I understand these are made, as a rule, by the engineering officer in command of the district, or at his suggestion.
Major-General MEWBURN:	That may
have 'been some time ago, but not now.

I am sure hon. members and the country will he glad to hear of the minister's declaration. When day labour is employed who selects the men? For instance, when repairs are made to the defences of the city of Quebec and the work is not done by contract, who employs the men? I know for a fact that everybody who applies cannot get work. There are foremen who have to abide by the list of the candidate or a friend of the Government.
Major-General MEWBURN: That is not the case now.

Yes, absolutely. Only a few weeks ago day labourers in Quebec could not he taken on unices recommended toy the ex-candidate or a friend of the Government. I am sure the minister is sincere in his wish to abolish patronage, and I mention this case to make more clear the necessity of doing work that involves a considerable expenditure by way of tender instead of by day labour. Who selects these day labourers?
Major-General MEWBURN: Work of that kind is left entirely to the engineer in charge. Surely we have to have confidence in our officers. If any patronage list is being used in my department it is news to me. I am heartily in agreement with my hon. friend as to the principle. As regards employing day labourers, the engineer in charge ought to be, and I think is, a responsible officer, not tied down by any patronage lists. I am not aware of any such lists and if my hon. friend will give me the details I shall be glad to have the matter investigated.

Has the minister given instructions to his engineers in the different districts?
Major-General MEWBURN: There was a general instruction given out some time ago that there should be no patronage in the department at all.

When was that given out?
Major-General MEWBURN: It has been given out on several occasions, from the Militia Council and other places. I have never given any written order.

Was it given out before or after December 17?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I think it
was before the election in many cases'. I determined when I took office I would have nothing to do with patronage.

Evidently the officers of
the department in some parts of the country did not understand the intentions of the minister. I know a returned soldier who lost his job the day after the election for voting for me, and I only cite that as an instance of the lack of strict compliance with the instructions given by the minister.	-

I hope the minister does not follow in the steps of his colleague (Mr. Reid), the Minister of Railways, who in a letter stated that Liberals and Conservatives who had supported Union Government would be equally provided for.
Major-General MEWBURN:	There are
no Liberals or Conservatives as far as I am concerned. The lowest tenderer gets the contract, no matter what his politics are.

Did I understand the minister to say that no written instructions were given to his. officers?
Major-General MEWBURN: I never gave any written order.

Does not the minister think that a written instruction would make his intentions more clear to the local engineers?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I shall be
very glad to take that suggestion into consideration.

I notice in the Auditor
General's Report that a man by the name of Samson, of Levis, received $415 for removing snow from the road leading to forts in Levis. Was that work done by tender?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I am informed that it was.

I would suggest that the country might save money if this work was done by defaulters or fatigue parties.
Major-General MEWBURN:	While they
are in camp?
Instead of placing the defaulters in a cell, why not make them work on the roads?

Every bon. member must appreciate the laudable determination of the Minister of Militia, but it is regrettable he does not implement it. Instead of simply making a declaration that he is opposed to patronage in his department he should go a step further and instruct his inspectors and engineers and those in charge of the different works of the department throughout the Dominion that all public works must be done without any patronage or pull. The minister, of course, is responsible for all work done under his department and he should see to it that the course he has determined on himself is pursued by his subordinates throughout the Dominion. I see that the first item of this vote refers to ordinary repairs and works. Has a very large amount of money been expended during the past year in repairs to different buildings throughout the Dominion? I have in mind particularly those buildings that are used temporarily as barracks for soldiers in training or waiting at different points in Canada for transport. Is that expenditure included under this item?
Major-General MEWBURN:	No, that
comes out of the $500,000,000 war appropriation.

How many of the engineers have graduated and how many have not graduated?
Alajor-General MEWBURN: I cannot say offhand, but all the officers of the Canadian Engineers are qualified1-every one of them, and at least two-thirds of the rank and file are technical engineers.

Referring to the question of patronage, I think the minister should state that he intends to write to all his officers or overseas, to all those men who have been in the habit of following the system of patronage in their district or city, that this practice has to be discontinued. I am sure that the minister means well, that his intentions are good, but we on this side, knowing how these things are done, are sure that the patronage system will not be discontinued until the minister issues strict orders to his

officers that there must be no more of this system within their district. It is no use for the minister to tell us to-night that if he has the opportunity of meeting one of these officers he will inform him that the patronage system no longer exists in the department. That does not constitute a general order, and it would be more satisfactory to the House if formal instructions in accordance with the minister's well-meant intentions as expressed here to-night were issued by his department putting an end to the system complained of.
Major-General MEWBURN: I might say that I took occasion to have a conference in this city with all the officers commanding military districts in Canada, and with the members of the headquarters staff here, and I laid down the principles upon which I propose to carry on the Department of Militia and Defence. The patronage- system was one of the strong points I took up at that time, and I made it clear that, as far as T was concerned, all patronage was abolished and I would not entertain the continuance of the system for a minute. There may have been some cases where the old system has been followed, but if so, I have no knowledge of it' I shall be very glad to take the advice of hon. gentlemen at any time for the betterment of the service.

From the answers given in reply to several questions to-night, it is quite apparent there is confusion between what items come under the estimates and what items came under the war appropriations. I should like to know from the minister what class of items come under the one heading and what class come under the other. There must be a clearly defined line between them, and to enable us to thoroughly understand what is done I think this dividing line should be clearly explained.
.Major-General MEW-BURN: All expenses pertaining strictly to what is known as the Canadian Expeditionary Force-that is troops proceeding overseas, and all the work done in connection with them, for instance, the fitting up of barracks, which my hon. friend was speaking of a few minutes ago, and accommodation for troops, except in a few items where minor repairs are being done on the military -buildinge-are all charged to the war appropriation of $500,000,000.

What about the permanent barracks?
Major-General MEWBURN: The repairs to permanent barracks, like Stanley bar-

racks and other similar buildings are charged to Militia account here, hut expenditures on temporary build|ings-for instance, there have been a good many armouries erected all over Canada that were fitted up temporarily for the Canadian Expeditionary Force for the housing of troops where shower baths and other such conveniences have been installed, and special hutments constructed in camps- I understand these have' all been charged to the war appropriation. Minor repairs to buildings are charged to the Militia Department, but large repairs, as I said before, are charged to the Public Works Department.

Are there any expenditures
charged to the -war appropriation covering salaries for payments made to em ployees of the department?
Major-General MEWBURN:	The salaries of temporary employees in connection with the war, that is all. There is one item, which I shall explain later on, in connection with the -permanent force which is chargeable here. That is on a different basis.

There are one or two matters which I would like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Militia, in connection with naval affairs, not by way of criticism, but in order to afford the minister a little information. We all remember with a very considerable degree of regret the disaster which op-ourr-ed in Halifax in December last. Naturally, that disaster occasioned a lot of talk, as would - naturally be expected, and some things were revealed with respect to Sydney harbour that, perhaps, would- not have come out had it not- been for that disaster. . Doubtless it is just as well that the minister should know this. Some short time after the Halifax disaster I was travelling on a train with a naval officer who spoke so familiarly with me, addressing me by name, that I did not care to ask wh-at his name was. He told me that if the people round Sydney harbour had known of conditions as they existed during the past summer they might have felt very uneasy. Hon. gentlemen know those fellows that come around wearing brass buttons and that play tennis and attend five o'clock teas-. They are not the men to look after a harbour, because in ninety-nine eases out of a hundred you cannot import men from across the oSean to look -after conditions on this side of the Atlantic. Those " haw-haw " fellows, those " Geordies," as they call them down in our country, those " gaiters," to use an-

other term, do not know anything about our conditions down there. Such men, for instance, as this man Pascoe, who has been down in Sydney for some time has no more right to be in charge of Sydney harbour than il have to be in charge of the Allied forces over in Flanders.

Grants to Associations and Bands-For grants to Artillery and Rifle Associations, military bands and military institutes, $25,000.
Mr. DuTREMBLAY: Would the minister explain how this amount is divided among the various associations?
Major-General MEWBURN: This vote has provided for grants for maintenance of civilian rifle associations and for efficient bands of the active militia, and also for military associations of the different arms of the active militia, and for grants to Dominion and provincial rifle associations. The civilian rifle associations have been practically all disbanded temporarily, so that no payments will be made to them. Bands of the active militia have also been very much reduced in number, few grants having been made during the past eighteen months. For the same reason, grants to associations, such as the Dominion Artillery Association, Dominion Cavalry Association, etc., have been discontinued. Grants have been made during the past two years to provincial rifle associations, such as the Ontario Rifle Association, when the organization has been kept up. These also have been much reduced. The .above estimate is based on the actual expenditure for the past two years, having been reduced from $50,000 to $25,000, which is the amount that may be needed.

I understood the minister to say that it might be possible to reorgan-, ize the rifle asociationsi during the current year.
Major-General MEWBURN:	I hope so.

If that is so, I would like to get busy on it.
Major-General MEWBURN:	We would
be glad to have the hon. member help it along.

We have in the city of
Quebec a most excellent military band attached to the R.C.G.A. Last year the band remained in the eity during the summer months, so that public concerts coold be given on the Terrace. But in former years, for some unknown reason, this band was withdrawn from the city at the very season when the concerts were usually given. I would call the attention of the minister to this fact and ask him if it is possible to see that these band concerts are kept up. The soldiers, I understand, are compensated to a certain extent by the city authorities. On account of the peculiar situation in Quebec city with the great number of tour-
[Major-General Mewburn.]
ists, soldiers and sailors there in the summer, I think it would be a good thing if the Militia Department arranged that the band shall remain in Quebec this summer.
Major-General MEWBURN: Was it not taken to Petawawa last summer?

No, not last summer.
Major-General MEWBURN: I oan quite appreciate the feeling of the hon. gentleman. I was under the impression, on account of .all the artillery having been concentrated at Petawawa, that the band had gone there last year.

It was there the year before.
Headquarters, Divisional and District staffs -For pay and allowances of the staff at Headquarters, and in the Divisions and Districts, $225,000.

There has been a good deal of criticism throughout the country with regard to the headquarters staffs. Ever since the war broke out members of headquarters staffs in the various military districts have paraded, particularly on Sunday, in staff cars. One of the greatest grounds for criticism, however, and the one of which we have heard the most, ie that a large number of the men on these various staffs have not gone to the front-indeed have never set foot outside of the country so far as military service is concerned- whiie returned men who are quite capable of filling these positions axe not called upon and are given no encouragement whatever to undertake such work. I quite understand that staff work is of a peculiar character, but it seems to me that it should not require more than five or six months' training to equip a man for looking after the staff work of an ordinary military district. Such training could easily be given to some of the returned men who have earned the right to wear the red tabs and gold buttons of which the member for .Cape Breton South (Mr. Butte) spoke.
Major-General MEWBURN: He was re ferring to the naval service.

They are prevalent also in the military service. What is the policy of the minister with regard to these staffs?
Major-General MEWBURN:	M.v hon.
friend, who is one of the fortunate ones who got over the top and got back again, must know that a large number of officers were retained in Canada against their will, *by superior authority, on the assurance that they should be enabled to proceed overseas. These officers, who have been prevented

from going overseas through no fault of their own have done dog's work in organizing, training andi sending reinforcements overseas. It has been no nice, comfortable, pussy-footing job, as some people think. I do not say that that applies to ail staff officers, but it does apply to the large pro-pcrtion of them. The magnificent work done by members of headquarters staffs is shown by the results attained by the units which have gone overseas. These officers, as I said the other day, are entitled to consideration; it is their misfortune, not their fault, that they have not gone overseas. I have laid down the policy, and I am endeavouring to carry it into effect as rapidly as possible, that returned officers, non-commissioned officers and men of other ranks, having regard to efficiency, shall in every instance get the preference. Of the officers appointed on the depot battalions which are being raised in each military district to handle the .men under the Military Service Act, over seventy-five per cent are returned officers, who have seen service overseas. Appointments of other than returned officers throughout Canada are being made only temporarily, with the distinct understanding that when a returned officer is available, the temporary incumbent must relinquish his position. With regard to the district staffs, there has been a good deal of replacement in some of the districts-not in all,-but I hope in due course there will be a large preponderance of officers who have seen service. I am out for efficiency-I think tha/t members of the Committee will back me up in this- and simply because I have an efficient technical officer fwho was Wot fortunate enough to get overseas-in many cases they have been medically unfit,-I do not think any one would suggest that I should kick him out and put a returned soldier in his place. I am however, trying to carry out the policy which I have laid down, having due regard to fairness and justice to all concerned.
Of those specially employed on headquarters staff 'at Ottawa during the war, how many >are officers of the militia and how many civilians?
There are no civilians except those temporarily employed, sudh as stenographers and so on. Clerks do not come under this item.
How many of the .headquarters staff officers are regularly employed and how many specially employed during the war?
I understand that some eighty-two are permanently employed on headquarters staff and in the various military districts.

How many on headquarters staff at Ottawa?
Major-General MEWBURN: Thirty-two.

How many are specially employed through pressure of work on account of the war?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Between
seventy-five and one hundred, I understand; I have not the exact figures here.

These are temporary employees?
Major-General MEWBURN Yes.
iMr. VIEN: How many clerks, stenographers, and under-employees?
Major-General MEWBURN: Some 3,200.

These are attached to the headquarters staff?
Major-General MEWBURN: In the different branches of the headquarters of the department at Ottawa

Assigned Pay and Separation Allowance, Records, Estates, Pay, and so on.

Sometime ago it was decided that no officer should be appointed permanently to any of the staffs or permanent corps. Has that order been carried out?	[DOT]
Major-General MEWBURN: No permanent appointments have been made since I came into office.

Of the 3,200 employees mentioned a moment ago by the minister, how many are male and how many female? I want- to know if among those 3,200 employees there are many who come under the provisions of the Military Service Act, and who should report for duty.
Major-General MEWBURN:	After the
Military Service Act came into force, every employee within the ages of those liable to be called out, had to report for service and undergo medical examination. I understand that in the whole (department seven exemptions were allowed, and those were only temporary exemptions, and there will not be a single employee of military age who will not enlist.

Were any officers of military age exempted in the city of Quebec?

Major-General MEWBURN:	I do not
know that any officers in Quebec were liable to service as privates.	x

I could name a few.
Major-General MEWBURN:	Who are
liable? Who ought to go?

Who will be liable to serve under the Military Service Act if they do not take advantage of the clause exempting them from military service as being militia officers. Has there been a change in the military command of District No. 5?
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes. General Fages was temporarily holding the command while General Landry was overseas. General Landry, on his return, has resumed command of the district.

Is General Fages still on the force?
Major-General MEWBURN: He has been retired on pension.

Full pension?
Major-General MEWBURN: Having completed thirty-five years' service, he is entitled to his full pension.

Has he been retired and is he receiving his pension now?
Major-General MEWBURN:	General
Fages has had thirty-five years' service. He was given leave of absence until the first of July when he will go on full pension.

Did he ask for leave of absence or was he given it?
Major-General MEWBURN: There was no place to put him, and in view "of his long and faithful service, he was considered entitled to leave of absence.

I wish to thank the Minister of Militia for the statement he made of his policy, but at the same time, I should like to ask him if it would not be possible to have some means of enforcing it. At the present time, we have, on various staffs, certain men. I presume, as soon as they see an officer who has returned from the front, they will not forthwith resign their position and say: " Here, Bill, take my job." Would the Minister of Militia . make some arrangement whereby the returned officer would have the advantage, if not of being-offered the position, at least of being made awrare of the fact that his particular qualifications would be taken into considera-
11 p.m. tion if he applied for a position at the time being held by some

one who had not yet been overseas? While I quite airpreciate -the great services rendered to the country and to the Empire by those who remained here to train the troops, there is undoubtedly, in the country and in this House, a feeling that those who went overseas to continue their training in the trenches are probably more entitled to consideration than those who remained behind. For those reasons I would ask the minister to be more specific in his declaration of policy.
(Mr. CURRIE: Hon members from Quebec perhaps have a certain hesitancy in asking this question. Is it true that the son of the Premier of Quebec has been in khaki since the beginning of the war and has not gone to the front? Is he on the Quebec staff, and, if so, how long has he been on that staff and why has he not gone to the war?
Major-General MEWBURN: * I am informed' that he is in one of the infantry regiments in the city of Quebec, that he has not yet gone, .but that he is going soon with the next draft.

How long has he been
in khaki?
Mr. LEMiIEUX:	A year last January.

Are the sons of the late
officer commanding in Quebec, General Fages, in khaki, and, if so, how long have they been in khaki without going overseas?
Major-General MEWBURN:	I believe
he has a son who has been in khaki for some time and who has not gone overseas.

Who is he?
Major-General MEWBURN:	General
Fages.

In case my hon. friend would insinuate that the son of the Premier of Quebec was not in earnest, I might say, for his information and for the information of the committee, that he joined the forces with my own son a year ago last January.
More than that.
He had an accident whilst on service in Quebec and he was operated on in New York. I came back with him from New York a few months ago, and I know he is ready and willing to go, and he will go soon.

I might say, in justice to this young lad, who is only a boy, that he was very keen. I know while I was minister, he was here trying to get his

training, but owing to his youth and other circumstances he was not allowed to enlist.
He had not finished his studies in the college at Quebec.
He was just a boy.

The reason I ask this question is simply this, that I have received a large number of letters from the city of Quebec in regard to the riot there, and all my correspondents, some of whom were anonymous and others not, laid at the bottom of the trouble in Quebec the fact that the military staff there was packed full of young aristocrats who had gone into khaki and had been holding down " cushy " jobs since the war began, and my correspondents could not see why they should be drafted while the " higher-up " officers did not go. I am glad of and accept the excuse given by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux) for Lt. Gouin.
It is not an excuse, it is the plain fact.

It was my endeavour while I was Minister of Militia to get- a number of these sons of what might be called well known families to enlist. I never found a particle of hesitation on the part of one of them. The son of Premier Gouin is a mere boy. When he first tried to enlist he was so young that he could not be taken.
What about Armand La-vergne? He was one of the leaders.

Everybody know-s I have a very high opinion of Mr. Armand Lavergne in many ways, and I am not going to turn from it here. So far as my association with himi is concerned, it is this:	He
has always, from his point of view, taken the constitutional aspect of the case. He took the ground in the nationalist campaign that, until Quebec had a voice and vote ,and say in the declaration of war and the making of peace, they could not, constitutionally, be sent overseas or volunteer to fight. Armand Lavergne has since that time repeatedly asked me, while I was Minister of Militia, to put him on, or order out the militia, for home service, so as to get over the difficulty of his breaking his faith with his fellow countrymen, and, once he was in uniform, to send him overseas. I pointed out that I could not do that under the law. I could order him out for home service, but I had no authority, until the present Act was passed, to send him overseas, and I pointblank refused to do so. I pointed out that he would have to volunteer of his own accord. He was anxious to
go' overseas. I am not prejudiced against Armand Lavergne. If what people say he has said is true, he should be treated in a different manner.	,
I have never yet heard, or never found any evidence-and I tried to get it-that he said anything except what might be called shooting off sometimes, when he got excited, and said things that were not absolutely constitutional. I have reason to believe that the young fellow, if he got an opportunity to-day, would go to the front and fight. I have a high opinion of him. I think he deserves credit, rather than condemnation, for his conduct in Quebec.

Is there a gentleman named Paquette and a Captain Durocher, who are on the staff in Quebec, who refused to go overseas?
Major-General MEWBURN: I could not answer offhand.

Aime Durocher, of whom we heard considerable last week, I understand did very great service for the Government during the recent riots-at least reports from him were read to us, and we were told he was a very good character.
There was a Duroche. over to the front.
He is there yet.

Do not confuse the men.
Permanent Force, $2,575,000.

Might I ask the hen. minister if the same policy is being pursued with reference to the members of the permanent force fighting in France, with respect to salaries, as has been adopted with respect to the men in the other departments? That is to say, a man belonging to the permanent force in France is paid according to permanent force scale. He is given certain allowances.
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes.

I understand an Order in Council is about to be passed that will make every man at the front dependent entirely on his military pay, without any additional pay from the Crown. Does that apply to the officers on the permanent force?
Major-General MEWBURN: That is the Civil Service.

They all belong to the Civil Service.

Major-General MEWBURN: It does not include the members of the permanent force.

I did not catch what
the hon. member said. I saw in the paper the other day that an Order in Council had been passed the effect of which would deprive those members of the Civil Service who had joined the force in 1914 in the First Contingent, of certain pay. I have m mind the case of my own secretary, Major Verret, the Assistant Deputy Postmaster. He joined the force in 1914 and went abroad. I am speaking of civil servants who joined the force in, 1914 on the understanding that they would get their salaries as civil servants, and their military pay.
With a guarantee.

An Order in Council
was passed to that effect at the time. Major Verret was decorated by His Majesty the King on the field of battle. He received his pay as colonel. If I mistake not an Order in Council was passed a few days ago denying him this double pay. Is that a fact?
Major-General MEWBURN: I think there were several scales of pay. I am not quite positive. I think the men of the Civil Service-and this had nothing to do with the .question brought up by the hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie)-who went overseas with the First Contingent in 1914 were to draw both military and civil pay, and I understand that there was a subsequent arrangement when men went over, I think in 1915 who got either their civil or military pay, whichever was the greater. I understand, if an employee in the Civil Service, is drawing, so much in the service, and his military pay is less, he gets the higher pay of the two, but not double pay. I understand the large bulk of the men who went over in the First'Contingent returned. They get the greater pay now. If the military pay is less than the civil pay, the difference is made up to them.

I was just going to raise the point mentioned by the hon. member for Maisonneuve (Mr. Lemieux). Remember, when a man joined the service there was no condition whatever arranged. The Government and the various departments arranged the matter of their own free will, and an Order in Council was passed providing that these men should get certain pay. I must say it is rather strange to drop off now the few that are left, especially when wm see the separation allowance

granted to the wives and families of officers who have never seen France, who stayed in Canada. Some of these men could not be induced to go to France, and others were anxious to go, but I understand the separation allowance is now paid to the wives and families of men in Canada who have never seen the ocean.
Major-General MEWBURN: These men in France all get separation allowance.

I am not speaking of that. I am speaking of the waste of money. (If it is a question of saving money on the one hand by cutting off the pay of the civil servant, or spending it on separation allowance to those in Canada on the other hand, I do not see why we should save money in that way.
I do not say that I approve of the first Order in Council, giving the salary plus the pay.
I never did.

But as a matter of fact an Order in Council was passed, and the men left with that vested right, that they would draw their salary and get their pay.
I have just mentioned the case of Col. Verret. I have another case in mind, a namesake of mine in Montreal. After having raised two companies, he left with the first contingent on the understanding that he would get his salary, as he was in the Post Office Department, Outside Service. He went to Europe and was made a captain. He married a Canadian nurse over there, and is there yet. He has been there four years with that understanding-that vested right. Is it right that the Government should now pass another Order in Council, and say to that man: "While it is true you left on that understanding, we have now changed our minds, and you will get only your single pay." I do not say from the beginning I would have given the double pay, but, as the Government had done it, it does not seem right to withdraw it.

I am very much surprised to learn that such a state of affairs exists. If there is anything this Government cannot afford to do, it is to break their pledge to the valiant men who are fighting for them. If it is a case of saving money. I think it would not be hard1 to find many places where you could pare off the small amount of money that would be saved! by breaking faith with these men. I think it is an absolute-I was going to say, disgrace-that the Government after giving a pledge to these men who went over there voluntarily to fight for this country, should now go back on its pledge after the men have gone "over there."
Major-General MEWBURN:	I do not
think there are many of them, but what the hon. gentleman says certainly has my sympathy.

There are quite a number of them "over there" yet, and it seems to me that the minister should delay final action on the question until it has been reconsidered1.
Major-General MEWBURN: Perhaps this might better be discussed by the Premier under the War Appropriation vote. I certainly think the proposal should be reconsidered.	[DOT]

It is not only Eatons who are continuing to pay their employees, but many of the banks as well. If you go into the Bank of Montreal to-day the clerks are all girls, and the young men who have left the bank to go to the front are still being paid a large portion of their salary. If private institutions can do that, surely the Government, which has given its pledge to these men, should not go back on them.

Is the present Postmaster General (Mr. Blondin) receiving hi3 salary
as a Cabinet Minister and at the same time drawing his salary as a colonel in the overseas forces?
Major-General IMEWBURN: I am informed on very reliable authority that he has not drawn any military pay.

He is relying on his salary as Postmaster General?
Major-General MEWBURN: I could not say as to that.

In the permanent force of Canada there were a large number of n.c.o's who went overseas at the outbreak of the war and through good conduct on the field have won promotion. What is the policy of the department with regard to these men when they return? It would be extremely difficult for a man who was a corporal in the permanent force before the war, and has since become a major or colonel in the C.E.F., to return to his position as corporal, and I think it would be well to set the minds of these men at ease by a statement from the minister.
Major-General MEWBURN: No policy has been determined on yet. I do not know myself what, is going to be done, but it is a problem that is confronting us and has got to be given very early consideration. There may have to be a complete reorganization; in fact, I fancy there will have to be a reorganization of all the forces. To-day we have the Canadian expeditionary forces, the overseas military' forces, the permanent force, and the active militia, and at the present moment it is doubtful what the status of a good many of these men is. I have given the matter a good deal of consideration, and I am thinking of appointing a committee of different officers who are now out of the service, and who have a thorough knowledge of the old militia, to go into the whole question. I hope that some of the old militia units in Canada with a history behind them will not be obliterated. No definite policy has been worked out, because other more pressing matters are engaging my attention at the moment. No harm will be done to thesh-chaps, however.

Are the members of the Permanent Force who are now with the Canadian Expeditionary Force still being paid by the Permanent Force?
Major-General MEWBURN: That is one of the items I referred to. The men in the government corps are being paid out of what is known as the permanent corps vote, except the field allowance and the difference-



in-rank pay, which they get from the overseas paymaster.

They just get the difference from him?
Major-General MEWBURN: Yes.
Salaries and wages, $260,000.

What comes under this item?
Major-General MEWBURN: This vote is to provide for the salaries of caretakers of armouries, clerks, charwomen and messengers. Additional help of this kind employed since the war has been paid out of the war appropriation vote. The increase of $10,000 is accounted for by an increase in wages to some of the caretakers. I can give my hon friend the details if he desires them.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Shall the item be carried?

No, Mr. Chairman do not
let. us be in too big a hurry.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: No one is in a hurry, but if no honourable member rises, the Chairman must declare that the item is carried.

I will ask the Chairman to be a bit more patient and to give us time to consider the items that come up for our consideration. I would like the minister to state whether any of these items have reference to the Ross rifle?
Major-General MEWBURN:	No.

Under what item of the estimates does the Ross Tifle come?
Major-General MEWBURN:	Under the
war appropriation.

Is Mr. McBain still the
caretaker of the camp at Valcartier?

I d'o not know who the caretaker of Valcartier Camp is, but McBain is a very honoured name. It is enjoyed by the descendants of Major McBain who fought at the capture of Quebec and settled at Valcartier. Ever since that time the name' has been an honoured one in the locality. I do not know the caretaker of Valcartier camp, or whether the oflice is filled by a McBain, but if it is the gentleman comes of a good family. Let me tell the committee that Colonel William
[Major-General Mewburn.]
McBain is a gentleman who has done yeoman service for this country since the war broke out. He has saved the department hundreds and thousands of dollars, and Canada, and the city of Quebec in particular, owes him a deep debt of gratitude.

Speaking of Valcartier
camp, did not this Mr. McBain make the expropriations of land there?
Major-General MEWBURN: It is not the same man.

Have the expropriation cases all been settled?
Major-General MEWBURN: I understand that all but three or four cases have been settled.

How much does Colonel McBain receive?
Major-General MEWBURN: The officer in question is not Colonel McBain, but Captain A. E. McBain, and as camp superintendent he receives a salary of $1,320.

The hon. member (Mr. Cannon) asks what Colonel McBain receives. He does not receive anything.
Major-General MEWBURN: I beg the ex-minister's pardon. I understood the hon. gentleman (Mr. Cannon) to say the superintendent.

Let us be accurate about it, he said Colonel McBain.
Major-General MEWBURN: At any rate Captain A. E. McBain, .superintendent of Valcartier camp, receives $1,320 a year salary. That is not one and the same person as the other McBain.
Now you have got it.
He belongs to the same family.

He belongs to the province of Quebec, and to a prolific family.
Transport and freight-Transport of staff, $20,000 ; transport of permanent force, $1.5,000.

Transport of the staff is estimated to cost $20,000, Whilst transport of the active militia is estimated at $15,000. The staff cost $20,000 for transportation and the troops only $15,000.. These items appear to be funny, because surely there are more troops than staff to be transported?

I understand that every time a staff officer travels he receives a requisition for transportation on the railway. Is that paid for dn the item under consideration?

Major-General MEWBURN: That is all charged back to the department and has to be paid for out of this vote.

Is payment made to the Government railways for the transportation of officers?
Major-General MEWBURN: To all railways.
Training: Areas-Purchase of land for training areas in the various districts, $50,000.

Will the minister tell us
what lands he intends to purchase for training areas?
Major-General MEWBURN:	There is
about $10,000 still to be paid on account of Valcartier camp. There are three or four small parcels of land to be purchased in Nova Scotia for defence purposes, probably costing between two and three thousand dollars. There are, therefore, at the present moment some $15,000 needed to meet existing engagements on account of land purchases, and a vote of $50,000 will leave $35,000 for any additional purchases that may be required during the year. It is possible that the negotiations for the purchase of the outstanding properties at Valcartier camp will be completed this year,-and the payments consequently met from current appropriation. Nearly all these cases, however, are before the Exchequer Court and it is quite possible that court may not render its decisions before the expiration of the fiscal year, and therefore the Department of Justice advise that provision had better be made in next year's estimates for the payment of the compensation dlue.

Can the minister give some
details as to the expenditure of the $200,000 voted last year?
Major-General MEWBURN: That all appears in the Auditor General's Report.
IMr. CANNON: According to the Auditor General's Report, much to my surprise, I see that Mr. Arrnand Lavergne has received a certain amount for legal services. ' Is he retained by the Militia Department?
Major-General MEWBURN:	He may
have been employed by one of the people whose land was taken, and judgment was given and probably this relates to his costs. I have no knowledge of his being employed by the Militia Department or any other department.

He is evidently on the
patronage list.
